title: Number of Unique XOR Triplets II
statement:
Pick three indices `i <= j <= k` of the integer array `nums`. The indices may be equal, so one element can be used two or three times. The choice produces the value `nums[i] ^ nums[j] ^ nums[k]`, where `^` is bitwise XOR.

Look at every such choice of `(i, j, k)` and return how many **different** values they produce.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every index triple costs O(n³), over 5 · 10⁸ steps for n = 1500. But indices may repeat and XOR ignores order, so only the distinct values matter: any three of them, repeats allowed, form a triplet. And all values are below 2048 = 2¹¹, so every XOR of them is too. So mark every XOR of two values first, then combine each of those (at most 2048) with every value.

## Approach

1. Put the distinct numbers of `nums` in `values`.
2. Grow `size` to the smallest power of two above the `largest` value; no XOR result can reach it.
3. For every pair of positions `a <= b` in `values`, mark `values[a] ^ values[b]` in `pairs`. The case `a = b` marks 0, which stands for using one value twice.
4. For every marked `pair` and every `value`, mark `pair ^ value` in `triplets`.
5. Return how many entries of `triplets` are marked.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 3]`, so `values = [1, 3]`, `largest = 3` and `size = 4`. The pairs give `1 ^ 1 = 0`, `1 ^ 3 = 2` and `3 ^ 3 = 0`, so `pairs` marks 0 and 2. Pair 0 with the values gives 1 and 3; pair 2 gives `2 ^ 1 = 3` and `2 ^ 3 = 1`. Only 1 and 3 are marked in `triplets`, so the answer is 2.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m² + S · m), where m ≤ 1500 is the number of distinct values and S ≤ 2048 is `size`: one pass over the pairs, then each marked pair with each value.
- Space: O(m + S) for `values` and the two marker arrays.

## Pitfalls

- Equal indices are allowed: `x ^ x ^ x = x` and `x ^ x ^ y = y`, so every number in `nums` is a triplet value.
- Count different values, not index triples.
- Size the markers by the power of two above the maximum, not the maximum itself: `1024 ^ 512 ^ 511 = 2047` exceeds 1500.
- Remove duplicates first; they add no new XOR values and only slow the pair loop.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `values` | the distinct numbers of `nums` |
| `largest` | the biggest number |
| `size` | power of two above `largest`; every XOR result is below it |
| `pairs` | `pairs[x]` is true when two values (possibly the same one) XOR to `x` |
| `a`, `b` | positions in `values` of the two numbers of a pair |
| `triplets` | `triplets[x]` is true when three values XOR to `x` |
| `pair` | a candidate XOR of two values |
| `value` | the third number joined to `pair` |

narration.2: Keep each different number once; repeated numbers cannot create new XOR values.
narration.3: The biggest number decides how many bits any XOR result can use.
narration.5: Keep doubling size while it is not above the largest number...
narration.6: ...so size ends as a power of two that every XOR of the numbers stays below.
narration.8: pairs[x] will record whether two of the numbers XOR to x.
narration.9: Choose the first number of a pair.
narration.10: Choose the second from the same position on; b = a means one number used twice, which gives 0.
narration.11: Mark the XOR of this pair.
narration.14: triplets[x] will record whether three of the numbers XOR to x.
narration.15: Go through every value a pair could have produced.
narration.16: No pair XORs to this value, so it cannot start a triplet.
narration.19: Join each number as the third member of the triplet...
narration.20: ...and mark the XOR of the pair with it.
narration.23: Every marked entry is a different triplet value, so count the marks.
